result:
I sat by the window, watching the rain trace delicate lines down the glass. The sky was a canvas of gray, the kind that made you want to stay in bed all day with a book and a cup of something warm. But I wasn’t curled up under a blanket. I was standing, staring, feeling the weight of the day pressing down on me like the clouds above.

What was I waiting for? Not for the rain to stop—it never did today, not really. The droplets would keep their rhythm, slow and steady, until they blurred into the sidewalk. Maybe I was waiting for the silence to settle inside me, that quiet where everything makes sense for just a moment. But silence is a tricky thing. It doesn’t always stay. It fills with thoughts, doubts, regrets—things you can’t put back in the box once they’re out.

I thought about calling someone. Just to hear a voice, to break the hum of my own mind. But what would I say? "Hey, everything feels a little heavier today" didn’t seem like the right opening. Not unless I wanted to hear, *Oh, it’s been that kind of day for everyone.* And maybe it had. Maybe the rain was collective—metaphorical clouds hanging over the whole city, everyone trapped in their own little apartments, scrolling, scrolling, scrolling.

I picked up my phone anyway, swiped through the messages. Most were meaningless—check-ins, memes, a recipe someone had sent. Then I saw hers. A text from last week, unanswered. *Miss you. Let’s catch up soon.* I hadn’t replied. And now, the guilt settled in like another layer of damp.

I put the phone down. The rain had picked up, tapping faster now, like it was trying to get my attention. Maybe I should go out. Walk through it, let the drops hit my face. Maybe the wetness would wash away something inside. Or at least remind me I was still alive, still feeling, still breathing.

I pulled on my jacket—black, too thin for the cold—and stepped out without an umbrella. The moment the door closed behind me, the rain swallowed me whole. It was cold, but not unpleasantly so. It felt real. Alive. The drops landed on my skin, ran down my neck, soaked through my hair. I closed my eyes and tilted my head back, letting the water wash over me.

For a second, I forgot everything. The texts, the silence, the heaviness. The rain had a way of doing that—it was blind to human worries. It just fell, relentless and indifferent, nourishing the earth, the pavement, the things that grew in the cracks. I envied it sometimes. Its purpose was so clear.

I opened my eyes and looked at the world around me. The city was gray and blurred, but there was a kind of beauty in the way the light caught the droplets midair, making everything shimmer like diamonds. A child ran past me, giggling, arms outstretched, trying to catch the rain in her hands. She didn’t seem to mind the wet. In fact, she looked happy. Like the rain was a game, a dance, something to be celebrated.

Maybe that was the lesson today. Not to fight the gray, not to resist the heaviness, but to let it touch me, to walk through it and see what it had to offer. Not every storm was meant to be avoided. Some were meant to be stood in.

I turned around and walked back toward my apartment. The rain followed me, dripping from my clothes, soaking my shoes. But I didn’t care. I felt lighter than I had in days. Maybe the weight wasn’t gone—maybe it never truly would be. But perhaps today, I had let it rain on me instead of trying to keep it out.

And that was enough.
